questions.text: Architect C prepared design plans for a shopping mall but the project was cancelled before construction began. Five years later, a real estate company obtained copies of these plans and used them to construct an identical shopping mall in a different province. What is Architect C's strongest legal position?

options.text: Architect C cannot claim ownership because the original project was never built, and the plans were not registered
Architect C must prove the shopping mall construction was done with actual intent to harm, which is difficult without direct evidence
Architect C retains copyright ownership and can pursue infringement remedies despite the original project never being executed
Architect C's rights expired when more than three years passed without project execution, according to standard industry practices

rationale.a: Incorrectly conditions copyright on project execution; the statute explicitly protects the architect's intellectual property whether the building is built or not.
rationale.b: Misunderstands copyright infringement standards; the infringer's intent is irrelevant; unauthorized reproduction alone constitutes infringement.
rationale.d: Falsely imposes a time limit on copyright; RA 9266 Section 33 contains no expiration based on time without project execution.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 33 explicitly protects the architect's intellectual property 'whether the object for which they are made is executed or not.' The copyright ownership is not conditional on project execution or time. The architect retains full rights to pursue infringement remedies regardless of whether the original commission was ever built or how many years have passed.
rationale.takeaway: An architect's copyright protection continues indefinitely even if the original commissioned project is never executed or is abandoned.

questions.text: A developer hired Architect B to design a residential complex. After the building was completed and occupied, the developer hired a new architect to design an expansion using the same floor plan layout from the original design without permission from Architect B. What legal remedy is most appropriate?

options.text: Criminal prosecution for theft of property, which involves proving intent to permanently deprive the original architect of their design rights
Civil action for copyright infringement, including injunction and damages
Administrative complaint to the mayor's office, seeking intervention based on local building regulations and professional conduct standards
Request for mediation through the real estate industry association, aiming to resolve the dispute amicably without resorting to legal action

rationale.a: Confuses intellectual property infringement with criminal theft of tangible property; copyright violations are civil, not criminal, except in cases of willful fraud.
rationale.c: Seeks an inappropriate administrative remedy; copyright infringement is a civil matter under intellectual property law, not a local government regulatory issue.
rationale.d: Suggests informal mediation for a serious intellectual property violation; while mediation may be attempted, the primary remedy is civil litigation under RA 9266.
rationale.correct: Unauthorized reproduction of architectural plans is a copyright violation under RA 9266 and the Intellectual Property Code. The architect may pursue civil remedies including injunctions to stop the unauthorized reproduction, damages for lost fees or harm to reputation, and recovery of attorney's fees.
rationale.takeaway: Unauthorized reproduction of architectural designs creates a civil copyright infringement claim allowing the architect to seek injunctions and damages.

questions.text: A client commissions Architect A to design a commercial building. The project is not constructed, but the client decides to hire a different architect to build the same design at a different location. What is Architect A's position?

options.text: Architect A has lost all rights because the project was not built, and the design was never realized in physical form
Architect A retains copyright ownership regardless of whether the project was executed
The copyright transfers to the client since it is the client's project location, and they have the right to use the design
The copyright belongs to the new architect who will supervise construction, as they will be responsible for the final execution

rationale.a: Incorrectly conditions copyright ownership on project execution; the statute explicitly protects copyright whether the project is executed or not.
rationale.c: Falsely assumes location determines copyright ownership; copyright belongs to the creator regardless of where the building is erected.
rationale.d: Misunderstands the copyright chain; the new architect has no claim to the original architect's intellectual property.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 33 explicitly provides that copyright ownership remains with the architect 'whether the object for which they are made is executed or not.' The architect retains intellectual property rights even if the project is never built.
rationale.takeaway: An architect's copyright ownership is unconditional and does not depend on whether the commissioned building is ever constructed.

questions.text: Which of the following must architects incorporate into all contract documents to provide notice of Section 33 ownership?

options.text: statement that the client assumes all liability for construction defects, which is a common contractual clause
clause identifying the architect as the copyright holder and restricting unauthorized reproduction
guarantee that the project will be completed on schedule, which is often unrealistic
An agreement that the client will automatically renew the architect's contract, which is not standard practice

rationale.a: Relates to construction liability allocation, not copyright ownership protection; this addresses a different legal issue.
rationale.c: Addresses project scheduling guarantees, not intellectual property rights; this concerns schedule performance, not copyright.
rationale.d: Concerns contract renewal terms, not copyright protection; this addresses relationship continuation, not IP ownership.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 33 requires all architects to incorporate ownership provisions into contract documents and other instruments of service. This clause serves as constructive notice to clients that the intellectual property remains with the architect and sets expectations for permissible use.
rationale.takeaway: RA 9266 Section 33 requires architects to include a copyright ownership notice in all service agreements as constructive notification to clients.

questions.text: An architect's service agreement is silent on copyright ownership and does not include any Section 33 notice. The client commissioned the design, paid in full, and received the plans. The client then licensed the designs to a third party for royalties. What is the most likely outcome of an infringement dispute between the architect and the licensing client?

options.text: The architect loses all claims because the architect accepted payment without explicit copyright notice, which is considered a waiver of rights
The architect retains copyright ownership and remedies under RA 9266 and the IP Code, though the absence of written notice weakens proof of client understanding
The copyright automatically transfers to the client who paid for the work, as payment implies transfer of all rights
Both the architect and client have equal ownership rights requiring joint consent for any use, which complicates licensing agreements

rationale.a: Confuses statutory copyright ownership with contractual transfer; copyright vests by operation of RA 9266 Section 33, independent of written notice.
rationale.c: Misunderstands copyright transfer mechanics; copyright does not transfer by mere payment or acceptance of compensation without written assignment.
rationale.d: Incorrectly creates a co-ownership situation where none exists; copyright ownership is solely in the architect unless explicitly transferred by written agreement.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 33 vests copyright in the architect by operation of law, not by contract. While architects must incorporate Section 33 notice in agreements, the absence of written notice does not strip the architect of statutory copyright ownership. However, the lack of notice in the service agreement may complicate proof that the client understood the restrictions and weakens the architect's position regarding the client's intent and liability.
rationale.takeaway: Copyright in architectural work vests automatically by law in the architect; written notice is protective evidence but not required for ownership.

questions.text: Under RA 9266 Section 33, who owns the copyright to architectural drawings and specifications prepared for a commissioned project?

options.text: The client who paid for the design
The architect who created the documents
The contractor who will build the project
The government through the Board of Architecture

rationale.a: Confuses payment for services with transfer of intellectual property ownership; paying for work does not transfer copyright to the client.
rationale.c: Incorrectly assumes the contractor who builds the project acquires copyright rights; the contractor is merely implementing the design.
rationale.d: Misunderstands the role of the Board of Architecture, which regulates the profession but does not hold copyright to professional works.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 33 explicitly states that drawings and specifications are the intellectual property of the architect, whether the project is executed or not. Copyright ownership belongs to the creator and author of the work.
rationale.takeaway: The architect, as the creator, always retains copyright ownership of architectural documents regardless of who paid for the design.

questions.text: A client who licensed architectural plans for a residential project in the Philippines wishes to construct an identical building in a foreign country using the same plans and specifications. Does RA 9266 Section 33 prevent this use?

options.text: No, because RA 9266 applies only to buildings erected in the Philippines
Yes, RA 9266 Section 33 prohibits all unauthorized reproduction regardless of location
Only if the foreign country has a reciprocal copyright treaty with the Philippines
The prohibition applies only to projects within the same province or city

rationale.a: Misreads the statute's scope; RA 9266 Section 33 restricts document reproduction without geographic limit, though enforceability abroad depends on foreign law.
rationale.c: Incorrectly treats treaty reciprocity as a precondition; RA 9266 Section 33 applies to all unauthorized reproductions regardless of international treaties.
rationale.d: Falsely limits the statute's geographic scope; the law contains no provincial or municipal boundary on restrictions against reproduction.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 33 contains no geographic limitation and prohibits unlawful duplication or reproduction of architectural documents 'for use in the repetition of and for other projects or buildings' without written consent. This applies to all uses beyond the originally commissioned project, whether domestic or international. However, enforcement of intellectual property rights in foreign jurisdictions depends on applicable local laws and international treaties.
rationale.takeaway: RA 9266 Section 33 restricts reproduction of architectural documents for any new project worldwide, though enforcement may depend on local foreign laws.

questions.text: An architect granted written permission to Client X to use architectural plans for a specific residential house on Lot A. The client later sold both the lot and the completed house to Client Y. Does Client Y have the right to modify and reuse those architectural plans for a similar house on a different property?

options.text: Yes, because Client Y now owns the land where the original house stands, which is a common misconception
Yes, because the permission runs with the property title transfer, which is not accurate
No, the license to use the plans is limited to the specific commissioned project and does not transfer to subsequent owners
Only if the second property is within 100 meters of the original property, which is not a valid condition

rationale.a: Confuses real property ownership with intellectual property license rights; owning the land does not grant the right to reuse designs for new projects.
rationale.b: Incorrectly treats the design license as running with the land title; intellectual property licenses are contractual and do not pass with real property transfers.
rationale.d: Misunderstands the geographic scope; the statute restricts reuse by project, not by distance from the original location.
rationale.correct: The client's right to use architectural plans is limited to the specific commissioned project. This right does not automatically transfer to subsequent property owners, nor can it be extended to different projects without the architect's consent. The original permission terminates when applied to a different project or property.
rationale.takeaway: A client's license to use architectural plans is personal to the commissioned project and does not automatically transfer to subsequent owners or extend to new projects.

questions.text: Architect D assigned her copyright in architectural plans to a design firm in exchange for employment. The design firm then licensed the plans to multiple clients who built projects in different provinces based on these designs. Which statement correctly describes the copyright ownership chain and enforceability?

options.text: The copyright remains with Architect D because Section 33 ownership is non-transferable, ensuring her continued control over the use of her designs.
The copyright ownership passed to the design firm by assignment, and the firm has standing to enforce against unauthorized uses and to control licensing
The copyright became public domain once any single client built a project based on the plans, eliminating exclusive rights and allowing unrestricted use.
The multiple projects eliminate copyright protection because the designs are no longer original, thus voiding any claims to exclusive rights.

rationale.a: Confuses the origin of copyright with transferability; while RA 9266 Section 33 gives the architect initial ownership, copyright can be validly assigned by written agreement.
rationale.c: Falsely assumes public domain status upon construction; copyright protection survives building construction and is not lost through legitimate use by licensees.
rationale.d: Misunderstands copyright protection principles; multiple legitimate projects do not diminish copyright; unauthorized use of the same design in multiple projects creates multiple infringements.
rationale.correct: While RA 9266 Section 33 grants copyright to the architect as creator, the copyright itself can be assigned or transferred by written agreement. Once validly assigned to the design firm, the firm becomes the copyright holder with full enforcement rights against unauthorized reproduction and the authority to license the designs. Multiple projects do not diminish copyright protection; each unauthorized use remains a separate infringement.
rationale.takeaway: Copyright in architectural designs is transferable by written assignment, and the assignee becomes the copyright holder with full enforcement authority.

questions.text: Under RA 9266 Section 33, is it lawful for a client to reproduce architectural plans prepared for one project and use them without modification on another project?

options.text: Yes, because the client paid for the designs, and ownership transfers with payment
Yes, if the two projects are in the same municipality and the designs meet local zoning requirements
No, it is unlawful without written consent from the architect
Only if the buildings have different purposes and the designs are adapted accordingly

rationale.a: Falsely assumes paying for services grants the right to reproduce designs for multiple projects; payment covers use on the specific commissioned project only.
rationale.b: Incorrectly treats geographic location as the controlling factor; the statute restricts reuse by project, not by location.
rationale.d: Confuses building purpose with reproduction rights; the law prohibits reproduction of the plans themselves regardless of the building's purpose.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 33 makes it unlawful for any person to duplicate or make copies of architectural documents for use in other projects without the written consent of the architect or author. This applies regardless of who paid for the original design or project location.
rationale.takeaway: Client license for architectural plans is limited to the specific commissioned project only; reuse on any other project requires the architect's written consent.
